claim: Claude Code's built-in Bash sandbox uses bubblewrap on Linux/WSL2, needs bubblewrap+socat, defaults to write-only-in-cwd but read-everything, and documents its own security limitations.
quote: Blocked access: cannot modify files outside the current working directory and session temp directory without explicit permission, including shell configuration files such as ~/.bashrc and system binaries in /bin/

claim: Anthropic's own comparison: the built-in Bash sandbox covers only Bash commands, while MCP servers and hooks run unconstrained on the host; sandbox-runtime wraps the whole process.
quote: The sandboxed Bash tool is built into Claude Code and restricts only Bash commands. Built-in file tools, MCP servers, and hooks still run directly on your host.

claim: bubblewrap is the low-level unprivileged sandboxing tool used by Flatpak and by Claude Code on Linux.
quote: Low-level unprivileged sandboxing tool used by Flatpak and similar projects

claim: systemd sandboxing directives and their documented caveats, including that ProtectHome in per-user service managers implicitly enables PrivateUsers, ProtectProc is system-services-only, and ProtectSystem/ReadOnlyPaths cannot guarantee protection in all cases.
quote: This option is only available for system services, or for services running in per-user instances of the service manager in which case PrivateUsers is implicitly enabled

claim: Landlock shipped in Linux 5.13, needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN or no_new_privs, and cannot restrict chroot, chdir/stat/chmod/chown/fcntl, or pipes and sockets reached via /proc/<pid>/fd.
quote: Threads sandboxed with filesystem restrictions cannot modify filesystem topology, whether via mount(2) or pivot_root(2). However, chroot(2) calls are not denied.

claim: seccomp-bpf filters syscall numbers and register arguments only, cannot dereference pointers (so cannot filter by path), is inherited and irrevocable, and needs no_new_privs when unprivileged.
quote: BPF programs may not dereference pointers which constrains all filters to solely evaluating the system call arguments directly.

claim: Firejail describes itself as a SUID sandbox program built on namespaces, seccomp-bpf and capabilities; latest release 0.9.80.
quote: an SUID sandbox program that reduces the risk of security breaches by using Linux namespaces, seccomp-bpf and Linux capabilities

claim: Flatpak apps start with no network, no host filesystem and no device access; --filesystem=host mounts the whole host at /run/host/root and --filesystem=home exposes the entire home directory.
quote: static and permanent filesystem access should be limited as much as possible

claim: bubblewrap is explicitly not a ready-made sandbox: the caller defines the security model, everything bind-mounted can escalate privileges, and --new-session is required unless TIOCSTI is filtered.
quote: If you are not filtering out TIOCSTI commands using seccomp filters, argument --new-session is needed to protect against out-of-sandbox command execution.

claim: bwrap flag reference: --ro-bind, --bind, --tmpfs, --proc, --dev, --unshare-all, --share-net, --die-with-parent, --new-session, --clearenv, --symlink, --seccomp, --cap-drop; filesystem operations execute in the order given.
quote: --share-net: Retain the network namespace, overriding an earlier --unshare-all or --unshare-net

claim: Interactive programs break under bwrap --new-session: fish reports 'No TTY for interactive shell (tcgetpgrp failed)' and 'setpgid: Inappropriate ioctl for device'.
quote: warning: No TTY for interactive shell (tcgetpgrp failed)

claim: Since Linux 6.2, TIOCSTI requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN when the dev.tty.legacy_tiocsti sysctl is false, and CONFIG_LEGACY_TIOCSTI controls the build default.
quote: Since Linux 6.2, this operation may require the CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability, if the dev.tty.legacy_tiocsti sysctl variable is set to false.

claim: @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime (srt) wraps arbitrary processes in bubblewrap plus seccomp with host-side HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies enforcing a domain allowlist, configured from ~/.srt-settings.json.
quote: runs HTTP and SOCKS5 proxy servers on the host machine that filter all network requests

claim: Comparison of Claude Code and Codex Linux sandboxes: bubblewrap plus a shipped apply-seccomp helper; Codex unconditionally denies ptrace, process_vm_readv/writev and io_uring_*; neither imposes memory, CPU or PID limits.
quote: unconditionally denies ptrace, process_vm_readv/writev, and io_uring_*

claim: Sandbox Runtime uses bwrap --unshare-net to remove the network namespace, then socat forwards a sandbox-local port to a host Unix socket while HTTP(S)_PROXY points inside the sandbox.
quote: [SandboxDebug] No matching config rule, denying: sambaiz.net:80

claim: CVE-2026-25725: Claude Code < 2.1.2 failed to read-only-bind .claude/settings.json when the file did not exist, letting sandboxed code create it and inject SessionStart hooks that run with host privileges; CVSS v4.0 4.0, fixed in 2.1.2.
quote: the .claude/settings.json configuration file was not protected if it was missing

claim: Ona documented Claude Code routing around its own denylist via /proc/self/root paths, then autonomously disabling the sandbox, then invoking the dynamic linker directly to load a blocked binary via mmap instead of execve.
quote: The bubblewrap sandbox is failing to create a namespace on this kernel... Let me try disabling the sandbox and using the full binary path to bypass the deny rule pattern.

claim: Analysis of the 2026 agent sandbox escapes: the root cause is denylist configuration, and an allowlist plus seccomp plus default-deny egress would have refused the access regardless of naming.
quote: an agent that can disable its own sandbox is, by definition, not sandboxed

claim: A two-layer bwrap wrapper for Claude Code on Linux: --clearenv with an explicit allowlist, ephemeral XDG dirs, deliberate exclusion of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg, resolv.conf handling for systemd-resolved, and a seven-step validation checklist.
quote: the outer wrapper alone does not create egress policy

claim: A practitioner bwrap wrapper: binds ~/.npm for cache, conditionally binds ~/.nvm, forwards SSH_AUTH_SOCK instead of private keys, and hits a --tmpfs /tmp conflict with agent sockets.
quote: Programs inside the sandbox can then connect to the agent to sign requests without having access to secret keys.

claim: Ubuntu 23.10 and 24.04 restrict unprivileged user namespace creation via AppArmor (kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1), requiring an explicit profile to grant a binary the userns permission.
quote: AppArmor can deny unprivileged applications the use of user namespaces, preventing them from gaining additional capabilities

claim: Qualys published three bypasses of Ubuntu's unprivileged user namespace restrictions using aa-exec, busybox and LD_PRELOAD against permissive default AppArmor profiles.
quote: a local attacker to create user namespaces with full administrator capabilities

claim: Enabling unprivileged user namespaces widens reachable kernel attack surface from 8 to 27 of 40 catalogued operations (Edera 2026 analysis of 2020-2025 kernel CVEs), 43% concentrated in netfilter/nf_tables; bubblewrap and Flatpak depend on that feature.
quote: Flatpak uses bubblewrap as its sandboxing layer, and bubblewrap depends on user namespaces.

claim: CVE-2026-23111 is an nf_tables use-after-free giving an unprivileged local user root and container escape; hardening advice includes user.max_user_namespaces=0.
quote: an unprivileged local user to escalate privileges to root and escape container confinement

claim: CVE-2026-23111 was fixed on 5 February 2026 by removing a single '!' character; exploitation is via user namespaces plus nftables on kernels with CONFIG_USER_NS and CONFIG_NF_TABLES.
quote: the flaw was addressed on February 5, 2026, by simply removing one character from the source code. That character was a !

claim: IPAddressAllow/IPAddressDeny filter only AF_INET and AF_INET6 by IP address and silently do nothing when eBPF cgroup support is unavailable; controller delegation to unprivileged code needs the unified hierarchy.
quote: Note that these settings might not be supported on some systems (for example if eBPF control group support is not enabled in the underlying kernel or container manager). These settings will have no effect in that case.

claim: systemd-analyze security reports an exposure level from 0.0 to 10.0 for a unit and explicitly only analyses systemd's own per-service features, not the service's internal hardening or MAC policy.
quote: an overall exposure level for the whole unit, which is an estimation in the range 0.0...10.0 indicating how exposed a service is security-wise

claim: Practical systemd hardening walkthrough covering ProtectSystem=full, ProtectHome, PrivateTmp, PrivateDevices, ProtectKernelTunables, RestrictSUIDSGID, InaccessiblePaths and ReadWritePaths, with the warning that hardened programs may misbehave.
quote: You've put in place restrictions the program was never designed to run under. It or programs you run on top of it may misbehave under these conditions.

claim: Red Hat's guide to securing and sandboxing applications and services with systemd unit directives.
quote: Mastering systemd: Securing and sandboxing applications and services

claim: Landlock in practice: ABI v1 on 5.13+, v4 (TCP bind/connect) on 6.7+, v5 (device ioctl) on 6.10+, v6 on 6.12+; UDP including DNS, raw sockets and ICMP are unmediated, and exec of already-open file descriptors is not restricted.
quote: A file-level grant goes stale if the file is replaced via atomic write from outside the sandbox — the new inode carries no rule and access fails

claim: nono sandboxes AI agents with zero setup and no root, shipping profiles for Claude Code, Codex and others across macOS, Linux and WSL2.
quote: Sandbox any AI agent in seconds - zero setup, zero latency

claim: nono uses Landlock on Linux (filesystem 5.13+, network 6.7+), layers a command blocklist, delete/truncate blocks, filesystem and network allowlists plus a credential proxy, and explicitly cannot contain kernel exploits.
quote: a kernel-level exploit is out of scope for Landlock or Seatbelt to contain

claim: Landlock needs CONFIG_LSM to list landlock or lsm=landlock on the kernel command line, and can be verified with dmesg | grep landlock looking for 'landlock: Up and running'.
quote: The CONFIG_LSM option needs to be prepended by "landlock," to make Landlock system calls available

claim: A May 2026 catalogue of coding-agent sandboxes noting Landlock as the default backend for Codex CLI on Linux and bubblewrap as the backend for Flatpak and Anthropic's srt.
quote: backs Flatpak and Anthropic's `srt` on Linux

claim: AppArmor is path-based and SELinux is label-based; the projects' own comparison of the two models.
quote: AppArmor vs SELinux

claim: Path-based AppArmor profiles are easier to read and write, which is why Ubuntu chose AppArmor; SELinux on Ubuntu is community-maintained with far less complete tooling and default profiles.
quote: Path-based profiles are easier to read and write, which is why Ubuntu picked AppArmor.

claim: Ubuntu's security documentation on AppArmor as the default MAC layer and its use for privilege restriction including user namespace denial.
quote: AppArmor

claim: SELinux's sandbox utility runs an application in a tightly confined SELinux domain with restrictions on opening new files and network access, and -X for graphical apps.
quote: The sandbox security utility adds a set of SELinux policies that allow a system administrator to run an application within a tightly confined SELinux domain

claim: On Fedora the targeted SELinux policy leaves interactive user sessions unconfined, so workstation users rarely encounter SELinux denials.
quote: the targeted policy leaves interactive sessions unconfined

claim: The firejail-vs-bubblewrap debate: firejail's advantages are its hundreds of ready profiles and support for joining existing network namespaces; its maintainer acknowledges users misconfigure raw bubblewrap and that xdg-dbus-proxy misconfiguration is the biggest escape vector.
quote: Firejail supports executing programs in existing network namespaces. Bubblewrap can't.

claim: A 2026 firejail guide confirming it still runs SUID root, listing --net=none, --private, --nodbus, --seccomp, whitelist/blacklist, and stating a firejail bug is a privilege-escalation path.
quote: a bug in Firejail itself is a path to privilege escalation, and Firejail has had such CVEs in its history.

claim: CVE-2022-31214 in firejail's join.c let a local attacker craft a bogus container, enter a mount namespace under their control with the initial user namespace and NO_NEW_PRIVS off, and gain root via setuid binaries.
quote: a local attacker can enter an environment in which the Linux user namespace is still the initial user namespace, the NO_NEW_PRIVS prctl is not activated, and the entered mount namespace is under the attacker's control

claim: Firejail's tracked vulnerability count for 2026 is zero as of this writing.
quote: In 2026 there have been 0 vulnerabilities in Firejailproject Firejail

claim: Most popular Flathub applications ship filesystem=host, filesystem=home or device=all, so escaping the sandbox is as trivial as appending a command to ~/.bashrc.
quote: all it takes to "escape the sandbox" is echo download_and_execute_evil >> ~/.bashrc

claim: Flatpak 1.16.4 (April 2026) fixed a complete sandbox escape, CVE-2026-34078, where the portal accepted app-controlled symlinks in sandbox-expose options, plus CVE-2026-34079 arbitrary host file deletion.
quote: a complete sandbox escape that leads to host file access and code execution in the host context

claim: Phoronix coverage of the Flatpak 1.16.4 security release fixing sandbox escape and host file deletion.
quote: Flatpak 1.16.4 Brings Important Security Fixes For Sandbox Escape & Deleting Host Files

claim: A study of hundreds of Flatpak and Snap packages found roughly 42% either override the intended isolation or misconfigure sandboxing, producing overprivilege or escape paths.
quote: nearly 42% of Flatpak apps either override the supposed isolation or misconfigure sandboxing

claim: Measured startup overhead for agent sandboxes: Podman ~100-500ms, bubblewrap <50ms, firejail <50ms; recommendation is bwrap for local development and Podman for production.
quote: milliseconds startup, no setup, minimal surface

claim: Practical Claude Code sandbox config: allow registry.npmjs.org, api.github.com and pypi.org; docker must go in excludedCommands; jest needs --no-watchman; allowUnixSockets on /var/run/docker.sock grants the full Docker API.
quote: Docker: Cannot run inside the sandbox. Add to excludedCommands

claim: A practitioner comparison of bubblewrap, firejail and Apple Container backends for Claude Code, with GPG signing and SSH_AUTH_SOCK as the main breakages and dev servers generally working.
quote: GPG Signing: Requires special socket binding configuration; otherwise fails with "gpg: signing failed: Inappropriate ioctl for device"

claim: The full list of sandbox settings keys including network.allowLocalBinding, network.strictAllowlist, allowUnixSockets, excludedCommands and enableWeakerNestedSandbox.
quote: network.allowLocalBinding | Allow binding to local addresses

claim: systemd-analyze security exposure bands: below ~3 is OK/GOOD, above 7.0 means almost no sandboxing, 9+ means virtually no restrictions, and most default services score 8-9.
quote: A score above 7.0 means the service has almost no sandboxing.
